question: How can a repeated chord produce movement without changing its pitches?
intro: A high bassoon melody gives way to repeated string chords, rival rhythmic groups and a final dance for the massed orchestra. Stravinsky conducts his own score here, nearly half a century after the Paris premiere.

sections.label: The Sage · Kiss of the Earth

cues.title: A bassoon above itself
cues.text: The opening gives a bassoon a melody high in its range. Other winds gradually surround the line; this introduction begins with individual strands, not a full-orchestra declaration.
cues.evidence: Full score, opening and rehearsals 1–4. The report begins quietly and grows between 0:50 and 1:10. The instrumentation comes from the score, not automatic source separation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer at the podium
cues.text: The conductor is Stravinsky himself. Columbia recorded these sessions with its Symphony Orchestra in Brooklyn on 5–6 January 1960; the resulting performance is a document of his later conducting, not a recording of the 1913 premiere.
cues.evidence: Parnassus label booklet, p. 2, identifies performers, session dates and St George Hotel ballroom: https://media.musicalconcepts.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/28214506/PACL-95003_4-Booklet.pdf
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Lines rather than blocks
cues.text: Across the introduction, listen for short wind phrases that overlap without becoming one continuous tune. Keep one strand in your attention as another interrupts or prolongs it.
cues.evidence: The opening score combines separate woodwind figures. This is a listening strategy for the introduction, not a claim of an entrance at 1:15.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Uproar and the riot legend
cues.text: The Paris premiere on 29 May 1913 provoked a documented audience uproar. The familiar “riot” story mixes that disturbance with later, conflicting recollections: neither the music alone nor every reported incident can be treated as the established cause or course of events.
cues.evidence: John McFerrin distinguishes documented boos and hisses from the uncertain riot narrative in the Library of Congress recording essay, p. 1: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/TheRiteOfSpring.pdf. Van den Toorn, chapter 1, identifies Monteux, Nijinsky and the premiere date.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The introduction draws back
cues.text: After its accumulation of overlapping lines, the introduction withdraws. Listen across this quieter interval for the difference between a winding melody and the repeated attacks that will organise the next dance.
cues.evidence: The report falls from the 2:20 crest to quieter 2:30–2:45 windows, before a strong boundary at 3:00. No final bassoon note is pinpointed.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: One chord, displaced weight
cues.text: In “Augurs of Spring”, the strings repeat the same chord while horns reinforce selected attacks. The pulse can remain steady even when the accented notes refuse a regular pattern.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 13 supplies the string chord and horn accents; the report changes strongly at 3:00 and shows repeated attacks through 3:20. Parnassus track divisions put Augurs about three minutes into this performance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Count beneath the accents
cues.text: Try counting the unaccented attacks as well as the forceful ones. The written bars at the beginning of this dance stay in two beats: irregular emphasis does not yet require an irregular bar length.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 3, examples 15–18, analyses rehearsal 13 in 2/4: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html#d0e3499. The suggestion concerns the dance’s rhythmic method, not a particular accent at 3:45.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A chord made from triads
cues.text: The stamping chord superimposes E♭ dominant seventh on F♭ major. Its component chords are familiar; their combination makes a dense object whose repetition and accent matter more than a conventional resolution.
cues.evidence: The notated chord at rehearsal 13 and Van den Toorn’s examples 15–18 establish its spelling. This explains a recurring sonority rather than identifying a chord from the audio at 4:25.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The dance gains weight
cues.text: The later part of “Augurs” repeatedly expands and contracts its recorded intensity. Listen for how a recurring rhythmic idea can accommodate a larger body of sound without becoming a longer melody.
cues.evidence: The report rises markedly between 4:55 and 5:15, drops around 5:25, then rises again through 5:45–6:00. The measurements establish the broad contour only.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Repetition is not stasis
cues.text: As this dance approaches its end, compare the repeated accompaniment with the shorter figures placed above it. Stravinsky can keep one layer fixed while changing the length and weight of another.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapters 3–4, distinguishes superimposed and displaced rhythmic layers. This is a passage-level listening point, not a bar-aligned identification.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A quicker ritual
cues.text: The “Ritual of Abduction” replaces the earlier stamping with a quicker succession of figures. Short gestures change direction abruptly; a constant pulse need not produce symmetrical phrases.
cues.evidence: The score marks rehearsal 37 Presto. Reissue track durations suggest about 6:00; the LP report changes spectral balance around 6:10–6:20 and sustains frequent attacks through 6:40. The section boundary at 6:03 is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Avoid the regular phrase
cues.text: In this fast dance, follow the small rhythmic unit rather than expecting every phrase to last four or eight bars. Repeated fragments can be shortened, extended or interrupted without losing their identity.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 3, discusses the irregular groupings of the Ritual of Abduction, especially rehearsal 46. No particular bar is assigned to 7:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The circle begins quietly
cues.text: “Spring Rounds” opens with a quieter woodwind frame before the heavier round dance. The thin opening and the broad central tread belong to one section, rather than two unrelated movements.
cues.evidence: Rehearsals 48–49 show flutes, small clarinet and bass clarinet before the Sostenuto e pesante. The report has a strong boundary at 7:18 and quiet 7:20–7:40 windows, followed by a level and colour change around 7:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight without haste
cues.text: The central round dance bears the marking “Sostenuto e pesante” — sustained and heavy. Listen for broad repeated chords under the melodic line, a different kind of weight from the quicker stamping of “Augurs”.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 49 specifies the marking and repeated string/lower-wind accompaniment. The report’s 7:45–8:30 span has fewer detected attacks and an expanding level; those measurements support the broad placement, not a beat estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A collected folk melody
cues.text: The opening bassoon tune derives from a Lithuanian song in Antanas Juška’s collection. Lawrence Morton later traced further sources; the score changes their rhythm and context rather than reproducing a folk performance.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, pp. 10–14, discusses the Juška/Juszkiewicz anthology, Morton’s identifications and their limits: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html#d0e414
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The round dance expands
cues.text: The broad dance gathers into a sustained crest. Compare its heavy, connected motion with the sharper changes of the preceding fast ritual; intensity does not always mean a faster succession of notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises abruptly around 9:05 and remains elevated through 9:35, with one of the highest five-second windows at 9:25. The score supplies the broad dance context.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A thin frame returns
cues.text: The quiet framing music returns around the end of “Spring Rounds”. That withdrawal clears space for the next group of forceful exchanges; it is not the end of Part I.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 56 restores Tranquillo. The report falls sharply at 10:00–10:20, with a boundary at 10:02, before the rise at 10:25–10:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Groups set against groups
cues.text: In the “Ritual of the Rival Tribes”, low, weighty figures alternate with quicker material above them. The contrasts are assembled in blocks, so a sudden change can replace the gradual transition expected in a symphony.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 57 and Van den Toorn, chapter 1, p. 19, distinguish the rival blocks and their combination. The report’s 10:28 boundary and renewed attacks anchor the approximate start.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Listen for the collision
cues.text: Keep the contrasting blocks separate in memory. When their materials overlap, the complication comes from combination: a recognisable low figure can persist beneath a faster upper layer.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, pp. 19–20, explains the superposition at rehearsal 57 + 4. This describes the section’s method without locating that bar at 11:25.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Accumulation before the procession
cues.text: The later tribal music builds towards some of this recording’s strongest sustained sound. Follow the accumulating layers into the procession rather than expecting a complete stop between the ceremonies.
cues.evidence: The report identifies 12:05–12:15 among its highest five-second windows. The score’s tuba procession develops within the continuing orchestral accumulation.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Low brass, recurring cycles
cues.text: Through the Sage’s procession, tubas and horns sustain recurring figures above the continuing lower activity. Their patterns do not all articulate the same phrase length; orchestral layers, rather than one tune, carry the procession.
cues.evidence: Rehearsals 64–71 and Van den Toorn, chapter 1, p. 19, document tuba/horn cycles. The report sustains high relative level through 12:20–13:00; the heading at 12:25 follows the label’s approximate subdivision.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The kiss of the earth
cues.text: The massed procession gives way to the brief stillness of “The Sage”. Low winds and a held string sonority make a hinge before the final dance; the reduction is part of the ceremony’s design.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 71, Lento, and the following held string chord precede rehearsal 72. The report drops sharply at 13:05–13:10 and stays quiet through 13:30; its 13:08 boundary supports passage placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The earth dances out
cues.text: The final dance resumes with a fast, densely repeated orchestral texture. Strings, winds, brass and percussion contribute to the accumulation: the return of force does not bring back the opening bassoon’s unaccompanied freedom.
cues.evidence: Rehearsal 72 is Prestissimo. Relative level and attack activity rise around 13:35–13:40; the 13:38 boundary locates the contrast. Score p. 74 supplies the orchestral restart.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A stop, not a fade
cues.text: The dance presses into its closing attacks instead of gradually dissolving. Listen for the gap between the end of Part I and the separate, slow beginning of “The Sacrifice”.
cues.evidence: The report has a high relative-level window at 14:40, followed by a sharp fall at 14:45–14:50. The recording’s second part is a separate LP-side track.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

transitions.title: Winding lines become repeated attacks
transitions.how: The introduction’s freely shaped wind lines withdraw before the strings establish the repeated F♭-major/E♭-seventh sonority. The pulse becomes explicit, but the horn accents deny a regular hierarchy of strong beats. Stravinsky changes the organisation of time and the orchestral centre together: the chord is a repeated object, not the goal of a conventional cadence.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 12–13; quiet 2:30–2:45 windows and a strong report boundary at 3:00. The exact first chord is not aligned.

transitions.title: The repeated block releases speed
transitions.how: The end of “Augurs” gives way to the Presto of the abduction ritual. Moving string figures, brass support and short wind gestures replace the earlier stamping pattern. The connection preserves force while changing the rate and grouping of the attacks, rather than smoothing the join with a tonal bridge.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 36–37 and the label’s cumulative track timings suggest the join near six minutes. The report changes colour between 6:05 and 6:20. The 6:03 marker is approximate.

transitions.title: Fast figures yield to a wind frame
transitions.how: The fast ritual stops feeding new gestures into the texture. Flutes sustain a frame for the small and bass clarinets’ melody; the score marks Tranquillo before introducing the heavier Sostenuto e pesante. The contrast depends on reduced forces and a new kind of motion, not on a dominant chord resolving into a new key.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 47–49; strong 7:18 report boundary and low-level 7:20–7:40 span. Instruments checked in full score p. 45.

transitions.title: The quiet frame is cut away
transitions.how: The return of the round dance’s quiet wind frame does not become a long coda. The next Molto allegro introduces contrasting low-brass and higher orchestral blocks. Low register and strongly articulated rhythm establish one group; faster answering figures establish another. Their juxtaposition supplies the transition.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 56–57; the report moves from quiet 10:00–10:20 windows to a strong 10:28 boundary and a 10:30 level rise.

transitions.title: Repeated layers become a procession
transitions.how: The tuba figure has already begun before the procession’s printed heading. Horn and tuba patterns continue over low-wind and string activity, accumulating into a collective arrival. The join is therefore an overlapping reorganisation of existing layers, not the entrance of a wholly new orchestra on an isolated downbeat.
transitions.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, p. 19: tubas at rehearsal 64 precede the heading at 67. Report level stays high at 12:05–13:00; the label subdivision suggests 12:25, not a new tuba onset.

transitions.title: The massed sound is suspended
transitions.how: The procession’s accumulated layers fall away into the Lento. Bassoons, contrabassoon, timpani and a low bass underpin the brief pause in activity; a held string sonority suspends the action before the dance. The withdrawal makes the next burst of motion possible without a separate lyrical transition.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsal 71 and the held chord before 72; report boundary 13:08 and quiet windows through 13:30. Scoring checked on p. 74.

transitions.title: Stillness is replaced by repeated motion
transitions.how: The held sonority gives way to Prestissimo. Percussion and a rapid orchestral sweep launch repeated wind, brass and string patterns. The contrast is between suspended sound and renewed bodily motion; no gradual acceleration is needed to connect the two.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsal 72; strong report boundary at 13:38, following the 13:25–13:30 low-level span. The marker identifies the surrounding restart, not its first attack.

source.title: Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring, full score, Dover reprint of corrected Boosey text
source.locator: Part I, pp. 1–85; opening and rehearsals 13, 37, 48–49, 57, 67, 71–72. Approximate passage states, not attack-level alignment. The later corrected print is used only for these shared scoring features; the different 1943 finale heard in Part II is not mapped from this score.

timeline.note: The opening centres on the high bassoon melody with sparse horn support; other reeds join as the introduction unfolds.
The early introduction interweaves reed strands with sparse horn support; this snapshot does not identify a string entrance.
The first Augurs block repeats a string chord; horns reinforce selected attacks. First violins are absent from this opening block.
The abduction ritual combines moving strings and short high-wind gestures with brass and percussion support.
The quiet frame of Spring Rounds places its melody in small and bass clarinets against sustained flutes.
The heavy round dance adds repeated lower-wind and string chords beneath a broad melodic line.
Low brass opens the rival-tribes exchange; horn and bassoon figures answer before the higher orchestral block.
The procession overlaps recurring tuba and horn figures with lower strings and reeds.
Low winds and a quiet bass support the Sage’s brief stillness; a held string chord precedes the restart.
The Dance of the Earth launches rapid sweeps and repeated massed patterns after the held chord.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
